I am currently a Data Scientist at 84.51 in Cincinnati, OH. I am on leave from my doctoral program in Economics at the University of Cincinnati after the birth of my son!
My interests lie at the confluence of economics, history and philosophy of science, and especially spatial issues; I am interested in the ways that how social scientists think about the world and study it comes to shape it, physically or otherwise.
My professional career spans economic research, technical roles, K12 education (as a Teaching Fellow in the Alliance for Catholic Education). I have worked in math education and education research; tax policy, transit finance, natural language processing, and geospaital analysis to name a few.
However, throughout theses seemingly disparate topics, I have maintained my interest in the philosophical and historical roots of the way we research and understand ourselves; this research has been deeply shaped by my own Catholic faith and a variety of transformative seminars and personal experiences I have had the opportunity to participate in. In spite of these interests, often I find the most rhetorically convincing arguments to synthesize these philosophical concerns with rigorous statistical methods prized by social scientists (especially economists).
I have B.A.s in Economics and Mathematics from the University of Cincinnati, a Master of Educaiton from the University of Notre Dame, and am a Wolfgang-Mayer Fellow in Economics at the University of Cincinnati Carl H. Lindner College of Business.

title: Research
text:
My research is fairly disparate in content but attempts to utilize the techniques favored by quantitative social science, especially economics, to answer questions that the technocractic approach tends to elide (or… just disregard as problems in the first place).
For example, much of my work tends to center on the friction between supposedly rationalistic, ‘science-driven’ institutions and structures shape how/what we see, measure. For instance, some work touches on:
Spatial and institutional mismatch is the most developed strand. Official city population figures, metropolitan governance structures, and federal spending formulas all inherit 20th-century boundary logics that diverge sharply from where urban density actually sits today. The Sprawl Paradox introduces a corrected density measure; Transit Fragmentation and Transportation ROI trace the fiscal and mobility costs; Federal Reserve alignment asks whether research institutions reproduce the same blind spots.
Institutional persistence connects the spatial work to a broader question about why organizations hold inherited structures even when those structures misallocate resources. The Catholic parishes analysis applies this lens to canonical boundary law; the papal continuity project extends it to the documentary record of magisterial teaching — testing whether Vatican II represents the radical rupture its critics and champions both claim.
Language as evidence runs through several projects. If institutions encode their commitments in text, then shifts in vocabulary, readability, and rhetorical structure are not merely stylistic — they are data. The street names project reads urban morphology through suffix drift; the papal project uses ITS and diff-in-diff on a 150-year corpus. The earlier HathiTrust NLP work is the methodological precursor to both.
The essays and philosophical pieces collected below make the normative commitments more explicit — they are the part of the work I cannot, and do not want to, hide behind the standard errors.

title: Research
text:
Research Projects

Mimetic Contagion and Collective Violence
Spatial evidence from lynching in the US Cotton Belt, 1884–1936
René Girard’s theory of mimetic contagion holds that collective violence spreads through social imitation — communities copy neighboring communities’ scapegoating, not just their grievances. This project provides the first systematic quantitative test of that claim, using a county-year panel of 2,614 Black lynching victims in the Cotton Belt (Tolnay-Beck + Seguin-Rigby combined). A spatial lag model with two-way fixed effects finds ρ = +0.054 (p < 0.001) under geographic adjacency — a near-doubling of lynching probability when neighboring counties lynched in the prior year. The core contribution is methodological: replacing the geographic weight matrix with three alternatives (railroad network, newspaper co-circulation, denominational similarity) to ask which transmission channel actually carried the contagion. Newspaper co-coverage produces the largest ρ (+0.101, p < 0.001), 88% above the geographic estimate; railroad (ρ=+0.041, p=0.041) and denomination (ρ=+0.041, p=0.019) channels also show significant effects. Mimesis traveled most powerfully through information networks — validating and extending Testa & Williams (QJE 2026) from elite signaling to horizontal crowd-to-crowd imitation.

Spatial Econometrics Historical Political Economy Girardian Theory Python



The Sprawl Paradox
Redefining American Urbanity Through Density
US city population rankings are distorted by arbitrary political consolidations — Indianapolis, Columbus, and Louisville absorbed their suburbs wholesale; Boston and San Francisco could not. The result rewards administrative reach over actual density. This project introduces the True Urban Core (TUC): contiguous population in Census tracts exceeding 10,000 persons per square mile, the threshold associated with transit viability and walkable commercial corridors. When applied consistently, cities like Phoenix and Indianapolis drop sharply while Boston, SF, and DC emerge as the nation’s true urban heavyweights. A companion analysis extends the framework to the OKI region’s fiscal geography, showing that urban tracts generate roughly 17× more property tax revenue per acre than sprawl tracts while receiving less federal transportation investment per acre.

Urban Economics Geospatial Analysis Census R



Transit Fragmentation
Quantifying Governance Friction in US Metropolitan Transit
In many US metro areas, transit service is divided among multiple independent authorities following legacy municipal boundaries rather than modern commuting patterns. This project introduces the Transit Fragmentation Index (TFI) — the inverse of a ridership-weighted HHI across agencies within each urbanized area — to quantify this institutional friction. Using 2023 National Transit Database data across 480+ urbanized areas, the analysis finds that fragmented regions suffer a persistent ridership penalty relative to consolidated systems of comparable size, even controlling for density, income, and built environment. In regions like Northern Kentucky and suburban Detroit, fragmentation accounts for a 55–79% loss in transit market share compared to demographically matched neighborhoods served by unified agencies.

Urban Economics Transportation Institutional Analysis R · Python

This analysis is now integrated into the Sprawl Paradox project as a case study in the fiscal consequences of boundary distortion. The standalone site remains as an archive.

Public Finance Transportation Geospatial R · Python



Brent Spence Bridge: Home Price Event Study
An event study tracking residential home price responses to major Brent Spence Bridge corridor milestones — federal grant announcement, contractor award, groundbreaking. Identifies a significant “landing zone” effect: ZIP codes within 1 mile of the I-75/BSB corridor outperformed the broader Cincinnati–Northern Kentucky market by roughly 8.5 percentage points since the 2020 fire.

Real Estate Economics Event Study Time Series R



Canonical Rigidity: US Catholic Parishes
Spatial Mismatch and Institutional Boundaries in the US Catholic Church
A spatial econometric study of how 19th-century parish boundary structures misallocate sacramental services across modern urban demographics. Uses Voronoi tessellations to construct “natural market area” counterfactuals against canonical parish boundaries, quantifying spatial leakage where parishioners bypass assigned parishes for closer alternatives. A companion analysis estimates the opportunity cost of underutilized surface parking in high-density cores using Overture Maps building footprints.

Spatial Econometrics Urban Land Use R · Python



Continuity and Rupture in Papal Teaching
Did Vatican II Break with Tradition? A Text-as-Data Test
The “rupture narrative” holds that the Second Vatican Council (1962–65) marked a decisive break in Catholic teaching — celebrated by progressive Catholics, lamented by traditionalists, and largely taken for granted by both. This project tests that claim empirically against 150 years of papal encyclicals. Using interrupted time series (ITS), difference-in-differences, and within-tradition cosine similarity, the analysis asks whether Vatican II produced a detectable discontinuity in the style, complexity, vocabulary, and thematic emphasis of magisterial documents — or whether the textual record supports the hermeneutics of continuity advanced by Benedict XVI.
The analysis spans six traditions (Catholic, LDS, Anglican, SBC, Orthodox, and USCCB) and a corpus of nearly 2,000 documents. Across most measures, the Catholic encyclical series shows less discontinuity at 1965 than peer Christian traditions show at their own watershed moments. USCCB pastoral letters — which post-date the Council and thus cannot serve as a pre/post control — track Roman encyclicals closely in complexity and style, suggesting downstream coherence rather than rupture.
The project is methodologically careful about identification: regression discontinuity is rejected as a primary approach because popes demonstrably time documents strategically, violating the no-manipulation assumption (Paul VI held Humanae Vitae through the Council itself). ITS with robust standard errors is the preferred estimator.

Text Analysis ITS · DiD Catholic Studies NLP Python



What’s in a Street Name?
How street suffix types lost their meaning across eras of American development
Street suffixes — Road, Court, Boulevard, Lane — once carried typological meaning. This analysis tests empirically whether that meaning persists, using OpenStreetMap geometry across four states (Ohio, Kentucky, Rhode Island, Connecticut) cross-referenced with Census building-era data. The core finding: by the 1980s, most suffixes are statistically indistinguishable on intersection density and segment length. A divergence score benchmarks each suffix against its pre-modern archetype. Road remains the most honest suffix; Boulevard has drifted the farthest from its original form.
A spatial mimesis extension asks whether cul-de-sac adoption spread by neighborhood copying. Year-by-year OLS across 207,000 block groups finds mimetic spillover β rising from 0.60 in 1940 to a peak of 0.90 in the early 1980s — the height of the planning monoculture — then falling to 0.67 by 2010 as New Urbanism eroded the dominant design vocabulary.

Urban Morphology OSM Spatial Econometrics Geospatial Analysis Python



Federal Reserve Research Alignment
Do Fed Banks Study What Their Districts Produce?
Topic-models ~18,300 Federal Reserve working papers (2010–2024) using keyATM with 10 seeded topics, then correlates each Bank’s research portfolio against district industry composition from BLS QCEW data. Midwest Feds show the strongest alignment; Boston, Philadelphia, and San Francisco are most misaligned, with research portfolios diverging substantially from local economic specialization. The Dallas Fed’s near-zero energy research score — despite oil and gas dominating district employment — appears to reflect that San Francisco captures climate and grid research under the same topic label.

Topic Modeling Federal Reserve NLP R

title: Research Agenda
text:
American metropolitan institutions — governance structures, investment patterns, and knowledge production — are systematically miscalibrated to the actual spatial distribution of urban economic density. My dissertation documents three dimensions of this misalignment and their welfare consequences.
The measurement problem comes first: official political boundaries obscure where density actually lives, providing a distorted basis for every institutional decision downstream. Papers Two and Three then ask what happens when governance and fiscal allocation inherit that distortion. A fourth strand — still in early development — asks whether even knowledge production institutions reproduce the same miscalibration.

title: Research Agenda
text:
Paper One · The Sprawl Paradox
Redefining American Urbanity Through Density
Working paper →
Conventional US city population rankings are artifacts of 20th-century boundary consolidations, not measures of urban intensity. Indianapolis, Columbus, and Louisville absorbed their suburbs wholesale; Boston and San Francisco could not. The result is a ranking system where a 900,000-person metro that is 85% low-density exurb ranks above a 400,000-person metro that is almost entirely dense urban fabric.
This paper introduces the True Urban Core (TUC): the contiguous population residing in Census tracts exceeding 10,000 persons per square mile, a threshold consistent with the literature on transit viability, pedestrian activity, and agglomeration returns. When applied uniformly, the TUC reranking is dramatic. Phoenix, Indianapolis, and Louisville collapse; Boston, San Francisco, and Washington D.C. rise to the top tier. The analysis also decomposes the “consolidation premium” — the share of a city’s official population attributable to absorbed low-density territory — for all 100 largest MSAs.
Contribution: Provides the measurement foundation for Papers Two and Three. Both downstream papers inherit the boundary-distortion problem; TUC offers a corrected spatial baseline.

title: Research Agenda
section: Paper Two · The Fiscal and Governance Costs of Fragmentation
text:
Paper Two · The Fiscal and Governance Costs of Fragmentation
Transit Governance Friction and the Cross-Subsidy of Sprawl
Transit Fragmentation → · Transportation ROI →
This paper has two empirical exercises united by a single argument: when metropolitan governance and fiscal allocation are organized around political rather than economic boundaries, dense areas pay and dispersed areas benefit.
Exercise A — Transit Fragmentation Index (TFI): Using 2023 National Transit Database data across 480+ urbanized areas, I construct the TFI as the inverse of a ridership-weighted Herfindahl-Hirschman Index across transit agencies. Highly fragmented regions (e.g., San Francisco Bay Area, TFI: 17.0) exhibit significantly lower per-capita ridership than similarly-sized consolidated systems (e.g., New York, TFI: 6.7), controlling for density, income, and land area. The mechanism is Coasian: fragmentation introduces transaction costs at agency interfaces — incompatible fares, misaligned schedules, duplicated overhead — that act as a per-trip tax on riders in polycentric or cross-boundary commuting patterns.
Exercise B — Fiscal ROI of Transportation Investment: Within the 8-county OKI region, urban tracts generate approximately 17× more property tax revenue per acre than low-density tracts, yet receive the lowest per-acre federal transportation investment. I construct tract-level fiscal productivity measures (estimated property tax yield per acre) and match them to USASpending.gov federal award data geocoded to census geographies. The cross-density comparison reveals a structural cross-subsidy: the fiscal surplus generated by high-density urban land partially offsets the infrastructure maintenance liabilities of low-density periphery.
Contribution: Connects institutional fragmentation theory to observable welfare costs in two domains — mobility and fiscal geography — and documents that both pathologies are larger in metros with greater true-urban/official-boundary divergence (from Paper One).

title: Research Agenda
text:
Paper Three · Research Without Place
Do Federal Reserve Banks Study What Their Districts Produce?
Working paper →
If spatial misalignment affects governance and fiscal institutions, does it also affect epistemic institutions with explicit regional mandates? The Federal Reserve System offers a clean test: twelve Banks, each with a defined geographic district and a research department whose formal charge includes monitoring local economic conditions.
Using the OpenAlex API, I assemble a corpus of approximately 18,300 Fed working papers published between 2010 and 2024. I apply a keyword-assisted topic model (keyATM) with 10 seeded topics — Agriculture, Energy, Finance, Housing, Labor, Manufacturing, Monetary Policy, Technology, Trade, Inequality — and compute each Bank’s research portfolio as a probability vector over topics. I then construct each Bank’s district economic profile from BLS QCEW 2022 county-level employment data, aggregated using official Fed district–county crosswalks.
The alignment score — the Pearson correlation between a Bank’s research vector and its district employment vector — reveals striking heterogeneity. Midwest Banks (St. Louis, Kansas City, Minneapolis) are the most aligned; Boston, Philadelphia, and San Francisco are the most misaligned, with research portfolios that diverge substantially from local specialization. Energy is near zero despite Dallas’s dominant position in oil and gas employment; the explanation appears to be that San Francisco’s “energy” topic mass captures climate and grid research rather than fossil fuels.
Contribution: Extends the spatial misalignment thesis from service delivery institutions to knowledge production. Suggests that institutional geography is sticky not just in infrastructure and governance but in the questions economists choose to ask.

title: Research Agenda
text:
Connecting Thread
Each paper documents a different institutional response to the same underlying condition: American metropolitan space is organized around political jurisdictions that were drawn for historical, legal, and political reasons with little regard for the functional economic geography they overlay. The TUC establishes the extent of that divergence. The fragmentation and ROI papers show its costs in mobility and public finance. The Fed paper asks whether the researchers charged with understanding regional economies have themselves been captured by the same boundary logic.
Taken together, the three papers argue that the welfare costs of spatial misclassification are not limited to any single domain — they are a systemic feature of how American metropolitan institutions are designed and maintained.
